newsitem.title: USA: Senate budget amendment vote on razor's edge.
newsitem.headline: Senate budget amendment vote on razor's edge.

text.p: A key Democratic senator announced on Thursday he will vote against a balanced budget amendment to the United States Constitution, raising doubts that Republicans can prevail in next week's crucial vote.
Freshman Sen. Tim Johnson of South Dakota, who had voted for the amendment during his House career, said he was now concerned it would jeopardise future Social Security benefits.

"In the past I have supported a version similar to this (Republican) amendment, but I cannot continue doing so knowing that it will jeopardise Social Security as well as the ability of the government to set aside funds for disasters, recessions or other crises," Johnson said in a statement.

With Johnson's name in the "no" column, Republicans cannot afford to lose any more potential support. By their method of vote projections, passage would now be on a razor-thin 67-33 margin, exactly the two-thirds majority vote required.

The proposed amendment would require the government to balance its budget each year during peacetime and would make it harder for Congress to raise taxes, approve deficit spending or borrow more money.

A constitutional amendment must clear the House and Senate by two-thirds majority and must be ratified by 38 of 50 states. Republican leaders had been looking to the Senate to lend momentum to the amendment in the House this month. The vote in that body was also thought to be too close to call.

The fate of the amendment, which Republican leaders have made a priority for the year, now hinges on two other freshmen Democratic senators -- Robert Torricelli of New Jersey and Mary Landrieu of Louisiana -- who have not declared their votes. Both have said they favour adoption of a Constitutional amendment requiring that the budget be balanced annually. They have also raised concerns about the future of Social Security.

"I still expect the vote on the balanced budget amendment to be very, very close. At this point, it's too close to call," Senate Democratic Leader Tom Daschle of South Dakota said after Johnson's announcement.
During the Senate debate over the past two weeks, Republicans charged their opponents had raised the Social Security issue only as a scare tactic to defeat the amendment.

Johnson said he had been convinced by a report from the non-partisan Congressional Research Service that questioned whether Social Security trust funds could be used to pay benefits in the next century when the huge baby-boom generation retires.

"In light of this very troubling and explosive report, I cannot, at this time, offer my support for the Hatch amendment," Johnson said. He could vote for the amendment if Congress agreed to exempt Social Security and to allow adjustments during recessions, he said.
Senate Judiciary Committee member Orrin Hatch, a Utah Republican, is the main author of the proposed balanced budget amendment to the United States Constitution.
Hatch and other Republicans had countered that report with a separate letter from the CRS that said Social Security benefits could be paid if other surpluses were available to pay government bills.

White House spokesman Mike McCurry, speaking to reporters before the official announcement, praised Johnson: "You know that he (the president) has expressed his concerns and objections to a constitutional amendment, so obviously a courageous stand by Sen. Johnson on that matter would be most welcome," McCurry said.

Republican leaders of the Senate have scheduled for next week votes on Democratic alternatives to exempt Social Security and make other changes to the amendment and a final vote on the amendment itself.
